The Mud sunfish (Acantharchus pomotis) exhibits a relatively modest maximum body size, with individuals attaining an ultimate total length of approximately 21 centimeters [Li = approximately 21 centimeters] based on field surveys of adult specimens from Atlantic Coastal Plain drainages. Newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal eggs measuring roughly 0.7 millimeters in diameter, and the corresponding wet weight at birth for a freshly eclosed yolk-sac larva is calculated at 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a value reflecting the limited endogenous yolk reserves available to support the endotrophic larval phase. Following yolk-sac resorption and the onset of exogenous feeding, these prolarvae embark on a pelagic larval phase characterized by rapid somatic growth. The size at which sexual maturation is initiated, defined here as total length at puberty, has been estimated at 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters] from growth trajectory analyses, a threshold that coincides with the transition from the immature juvenile stage to a reproductively viable adult.

Reproductive output in Acantharchus pomotis has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions, with the maximum reproductive rate characterized through the combination of fecundity per event and spawning frequency. Gravid females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], with each clutch containing approximately 3812 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing approximately 3812 eggs] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This annual reproductive allocation is notable for a centrarchid of this body size, as the numerical investment in offspring is comparatively high. The relationship between maternal body size and clutch volume appears to follow a positive allometric trend, with larger females contributing disproportionately more to the annual egg production of the population. Such iteroparous spawning strategies are common among temperate freshwater teleosts, enabling individuals to buffer against interannual variability in nursery habitat quality and prey availability for their pelagic larvae.

The allometric scaling relationship between length and wet weight in Mud sunfish has been derived from a comprehensive morphometric dataset, yielding a parameterization of 0.01230 times the total length raised to the power of 3.06. Using this length–mass conversion, the ultimate wet weight corresponding to the maximum recorded total length of 21 centimeters is computed as approximately 137 grams [Wwi = approximately 137 grams], representing the asymptotic adult body mass. Similarly, the wet weight at puberty, derived from the total length at puberty of 11 centimeters, is estimated at 18.9 grams [Wwp = 18.9 grams], a value that marks the somatic threshold at which gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis are first initiated. This body mass at the onset of reproductive maturity is roughly 14 percent of the ultimate adult mass, a proportion that aligns with patterns observed in other iteroparous centrarchids where early reproduction occurs well before the attainment of asymptotic size.

Lifespan data for Mud sunfish indicate a maximum documented longevity of approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days] under stable thermal conditions of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] in captivity, a duration that positions Acantharchus pomotis among the shorter-lived members of the Centrarchidae, particularly when compared to congeners such as the Largemouth Bass (Micropterus salmoides), which can exceed a decade in age. The relatively compressed lifespan suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward early maturation and high annual reproductive investment rather than extended iteroparity. Senescent changes, including diminished condition factor and reduced gonadosomatic index, become apparent after the fourth year, with natural mortality rates increasing substantially in older cohorts. Parasite loads and accumulated oxidative damage likely contribute to this pattern of physiological decline.

Comparative analysis of the life-history traits of Acantharchus pomotis reveals a suite of adaptations characteristic of lowland, vegetated freshwater habitats. The species attains a maximum size of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters] total length, with an associated asymptotic body mass of 137 grams [Wwi = 137 grams], dimensions that facilitate exploitation of dense macrophyte cover where larger piscivores are less effective. The moderate size at puberty, 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters] total length, and the corresponding wet weight of 18.9 grams [Wwp = 18.9 grams] at that transition, indicate a relatively early onset of reproductive capability, allowing individuals to contribute to the population before facing elevated mortality risks from predation or seasonal habitat desiccation. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed as approximately 3812 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 3812 eggs per clutch] with a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] under a thermal regime of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], reflects a strategy of producing a large, single annual brood rather than distributing effort across multiple smaller spawning events. This demographic profile, coupled with a maximum lifespan of 2190 days [am = 2190 days] at 21 °C [T = 21 °C], suggests that Mud sunfish employs a bet-hedging approach, investing heavily in early reproduction to offset the constraints of a relatively short adult lifespan in a variable environment.
